newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Q2 slowdown seen uneven among Fed districts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Q2 slowdown seen uneven among Fed districts.

text.p: The U.S. economy has cooled in the second quarter, but a close look at the performance of some Federal Reserve economic districts shows the degree of that slowdown varies considerably by region.

Although not uncommon, the phenomenon adds pieces to the current economic puzzle since it suggests the economy might be moving out of the across-the-board strength scenario seen in the first quarter and into a more diverse environment.
"All in all, the economy here in aggregate remains fairly strong," said Raymond Owens, a regional economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.

Owens said prospects for workers in the fifth economic region -- which encompasses the Distric of Columbia, Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia and most of West Virginia -- remained buoyant as labor markets continued to tighten somewhat.

Meanwhile, the job market in the country's third economic district -- which includes Delaware, the eastern region of Pennsylvania and the southern portion of New Jersey -- appears to be calming down a bit.

"I think that in general we're going to see increases in employment to be much more moderate in our region," said Ted Crone, assistant vice president and regional economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.

"We saw some large increases in January and February, (but) those increases just won't continue through the rest of this year ... Delaware, for example, had a slight decline in payroll employment for April," Crone added.
In the manufacturing sector, the fifth district economy also appears to be more robust.

"Manufacturers, at least in our district, are looking for this rebound (in industry activity in April) to have a bit of staying power over the next several months at the very least, perhaps longer," Owens said.

In the third district, however, industry activity seems to be a little more sluggish. The Philadelphia Fed's most recent business outlook survey showed activity in the manufacturing sector fell to 1.6 in May from 5.7 in April.
Crone said the housing sector also seemed to be slowing in the third region, adding that that pattern was likely to continue throughout the year.

"The most recent building permits data were lower, indicating that the rapid pace in the housing market that we saw in the first quarter is not going to continue through the rest of the year," Crone said.
Crone said the cooling off in housing permits might be seen as a signal of what might happen to the rest of the local economy in coming months.

"Housing sales do stimulate a lot of activtity. When you see a slowdown there, then you see that we're not going to keep up that pace of the national level where we had over 5.0 percent Gross Domestic Product growth in the first quarter.
"Looking ahead to the third quarter, it's still hard to know at what pace we're going to be growing ... But it certainly is not going to be the rapid pace of the first quarter," Crone added.
Despite the apparent differences between the performances of the two economies, both regional Fed officials agreed that inflation remained a slumbering giant.
Although they acknowledged some scattered wage pressures in specific areas, they said no major price pressures have emerged so far on the horizon.
Richmond Fed's Owens said income growth in the fifth region is still expanding at a healthy pace, but he added that the phenomenon was not a source of concern at this point.
"Income is growing at a healthy pace currently in the district. (But) there is certainly no sign that it's going off track either on the upside or downside at this point.
"I would consider the current growth rate very desirable," Owens said.
The Fed last raised interest rates on March 25, when it increased its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.

The central bank decided to leave interest rates unchanged at the latest meeting of its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on May 20. The FOMC meets next to analyze the economy and deliberate on interest rates on July 1 and 2.
